title: Per l’aer perso
html_source: “Lost through the air.” Again, a reference to wind. M.J.C. Hodgart points out in “James Joyce’s Ulysses: Critical Essays” that The nature of the “wind” in this case, consistent with Joyce’s frequent reference to the Hebrews and the Greeks, is elucidated by the Hebrew “ruach”, meaning, not only wind, but spirit, soul, mind, intellect, passion, as well as by the Greek “anemos” which likewise means wind and breath, the spiritual principle of human life, rational soul, disposition. Latinized for us English speakers, “The etymology of the verb “inspirare”, then, leads us to “to breathe into”, “to blow upon”, “to excite”, “to inflame”, “to arouse by divine influence.” The noun “spiritus” points us to “breath of life”, “spirit”, “soul”, “mind”. This all has to do with artistic inspiration. “Lost through the air” may refer to the fleeting nature of such inspiration brought on, perhaps, by the sight of three girls, the way they are dressed, and by the way they hang on to each other. How to capture that image while out for a walk?
